title: Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom day
hookLine: remembered each year, he is often called the shield of India

lines: NOT YOUR FAITH, NOT YOUR PEOPLE.
cards: Strangers arrive at your door. They aren't your people, and they don't share your faith. They've traveled a long way, and they're frightened.
Our families are being pressured to give up our religion, they say, and we don't know who else to ask. What would you say? Sikhs remember that this is what happened at Anandpur in 1675.
The visitors were Kashmiri Pandits, Hindu scholars and priests. The man they came to see was the ninth Guru.

teach.b: Guru Tegh Bahadur listened. Tradition says he sat quiet a long time, then said it would take the sacrifice of a great soul.

teach.h: WHO COULD BE GREATER THAN YOU?
teach.b: His son Gobind, about nine years old, answered: who could be greater than you?

So the Guru sent the Pandits back with a message for the officials of the emperor Aurangzeb: if Tegh Bahadur can be made to change his faith, we will all change ours. Then he set out for Delhi himself. He was arrested.
Three of his companions, Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das and Bhai Dayala, were put to death in front of him, tradition says, to break him. He didn't break.
In November 1675, in the square at Chandni Chowk in Delhi, he was beheaded. Gurdwara Sis Ganj stands on the spot now.
Sikhs hold on to this: he gave his life for other people's right to worship, a right he didn't need for himself. He didn't wear their sacred thread or their forehead mark.
His son, Guru Gobind Singh, later wrote that his father protected their tilak and their thread, and gave his head but not his faith. So he is called Hind di Chadar. Hind is India.
A chadar is a sheet, a covering, the cloth you'd put over someone to shelter them.
The covering of India. His own verses in the Guru Granth Sahib say, in paraphrase, that the wise one frightens no one and is afraid of no one.
Sikhs mark his martyrdom every year, in late autumn, with kirtan, and many visit Sis Ganj.

how: Sikhs mark Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom each year in late autumn with kirtan, readings and langar; many visit Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Delhi, where he was executed, and Gurdwara Rakab Ganj, where his body was cremated.

o: the Delhi gurdwara where the ninth Guru was beheaded
a Punjab shrine that keeps the ninth Guru's sword
the Anandpur gurdwara where the Pandits asked for help

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: came to Anandpur asking for help
who could be greater than you?

s: Guru Tegh Bahadur died defending the Sikh faith only
Sikhs remember him dying for the right of Hindus, who weren't his community, to keep their faith.
his son was about nine when the Pandits came
tradition says young Gobind asked, who could be greater than you?
Gurdwara Sis Ganj stands where he was executed

games.q: frightened strangers of another faith ask the Guru for help against forced conversion. what does he do?
o: tell them to join the Sikhs.
go to Delhi himself, and stake his own life on their freedom.
send them money and wish them well.
games.why: he sent word that if he could be made to convert, they would all convert, and went to Delhi, where he was executed in 1675.

practice: Think of people anywhere who can't practice their faith freely, or who are pushed to take on one they don't hold; no need to name a country, just let them be people: a family at dinner, a grandmother, a kid at school who hides what she believes.
If you pray, pray for their freedom, in your own words or simply with Waheguru. If you don't, wish them room to believe as they choose, and to be left in peace.

wordCard.voice: Sis Ganj. The gurdwara in Delhi marking where Guru Tegh Bahadur was beheaded, after he gave his life so others could keep their faith.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the covering, or sheltering cloth, of India.

carryVoice: Your line: a shield for others. He covered a faith that wasn't his own. Day one hundred fifty-five.
